Issued at 208 PM CDT Mon Jul 27 2026

Early this afternoon, a broken line of severe convection with 
embedded supercells is tracking east across the interior Chicago
metro area. Since the start of the afternoon, these storms have
likely been responsible for at least one tornado, if not a few,
large hail, and some road flooding. Latest SPC mesoanalysis 
suggests up to 5,000 J/kg of MLCAPE resides over NE IL which 
have been allowing for convective cloud tops up -80C reaching 
heights over 60,000 ft. This cluster had developed along a tight
instability gradient on the leading edge of a low level 
shortwave disturbance pushing across northern IL. The system as 
a whole is being carried toward the east with the synoptic wave 
while individual cells are tracking more southeastward with a NW
shear profile. With activity beginning to cross into 
northwestern IN as of 1PM, would imagine these storms should 
have little to no trouble maintaining themselves over the next 
couple of hours as they spread SE over our IN counties. All 
hazards will remain possible with these storms into late 
afternoon before moving away to our east including damaging to 
destructive winds, large hail, flooding, and possibly a tornado.


Depending on how long these current storms and isolated trailing
activity want to fester in our eastern CWA, we may see a brief 
relative lull in activity during the mid-late afternoon. 
Thereafter, additional thunderstorms may target our area along 
and ahead of a cold front during the late afternoon and evening.
Severe storms associated with this feature are already ongoing 
over east-central WI. Guidance has been of little help today 
going back and forth with solutions for later today. This 
morning, camps were backing off on additional convection this 
evening, but latest CAM guidance is starting to get excited 
again. It's not entirely clear to what extent the ongoing 
convection will influence the low level thermodynamic 
environment for later. Outflow from ongoing storms is pushing 
away from the metro into the outlying areas. Wouldn't imagine at
this point in the day that the unstable airmass will have time 
to recover much where its been removed. Nonetheless, the 
environment aloft will remain plenty unstable and supportive of 
additional severe storms later if parcels can be sufficiently 
forced. However, forcing along the front appears rather meager 
with not a ton of help from features aloft. Additionally, lots 
of deep layer dry advection, including through the low levels, 
will take place on the back edge of the shortwave between now 
and this evening. This will work against deep convective 
development down into northern IL this evening along the front. 
With this sort of instability though and with storms already 
ongoing, imagine it's rather likely we see at least some 
activity during the evening hours; whether it's severe remains 
unclear. The highest coverage during the evening is heavily 
favored across the eastern half of the CWA near and east of the 
track of the disorganized surface low. If storms can mature 
along the front later today, damaging winds will be the biggest 
concern with hail and flooding also a possibility. Little to no 
low level instability and unfavorable hodographs don't appear to
present much of a tornado threat this evening, even with 
surface-based storms.

Storms should move away from the area by the end of the 
evening. Gusty northerly winds will develop in the wake of the 
front late tonight into tomorrow, especially over the lake. This
will quickly generate high waves and dangerous currents on the 
lake and a High Swim Risk is forecast at area Lake Michigan 
beaches from late tonight into Wednesday morning. Some patches 
of fog may also attempt to develop in the wake of the front late
tonight, but not seeing much of a signal for any widespread 
dense fog. Rather, we may be stuck beneath a blanket of gloomy 
low stratus during the morning tomorrow.

The cold frontal passage will bring relatively cooler (albeit 
still warm) conditions to the middle of the week with lower and 
middle 80s forecast Tuesday and Wednesday afternoons. Regional 
high pressure will bring quiet and largely sunny conditions to 
the middle part of the week before another synoptic system looks
to bring more rain and storm chances to the region by Friday.
